title: How to manage game design documentation on Mac: a guide for designers
metaTitle: Game Design Documentation Management: Fixes for Mac Designers
description: Stop drowning in outdated GDDs. Learn how to maintain game design documentation on Mac with simple workflows that save hours every week.
intro: Game design documentation is often the most neglected part of a project, becoming a graveyard for outdated ideas. You can fix your game design documentation workflow on your Mac by moving away from static files and toward modular, living systems.
tldr: Stop writing massive, static game design documents that no one reads.
Use modular structures to separate design prose from balance data.
Adopt Architecture Decision Records to track why changes happen.
Leverage Mac-native tools like Notion and Obsidian to link your ideas.
Treat your prototype as the primary source of truth.

blocks.text: The hidden cost of bad game design documentation

Documentation is not just about writing. It is about communication. When your game design documentation is fragmented, your team loses time guessing intent. You spend hours answering the same questions in Slack or email. This is the administrative tax on your creative work.

Most designers try to build a game design document that covers everything from day one. This approach fails because games are iterative. When you change a jump mechanic, you must update the GDD, the spreadsheet, and the task card. If you miss one, the documentation becomes a liability. It creates confusion instead of clarity.

items: Rigid, long-form documents that are never updated.
Disconnected tools that make cross-referencing impossible.
Lack of context on why a specific design choice was made.
Different formats for different departments causing silos.

blocks.text: You do not need expensive software to fix this. Start by changing how you structure your files. Keep your prose and your data separate. Use Architecture Decision Records to log the reasoning behind major shifts. This preserves institutional knowledge when team members change.

Use a modular chapter hierarchy in Notion. Create a main page for your core pillars and link to separate databases for mechanics, narrative, and balance data. This makes it easy to update one piece without rewriting the whole document.
blocks.title: Modular Documentation

blocks.text: Tools for the modern Mac designer

Your Mac is a powerful tool for documentation. Use Notion for structured databases. Use Obsidian if you prefer a local, Markdown-based wiki. Use Miro for visual system mapping. These tools allow you to connect ideas rather than just listing them.

blocks.caption: Software tools for organized design work

faq.question: How often should I update my GDD?
faq.answer: Update it during milestone reviews or after major mechanics changes. Do not try to keep it updated for every minor tweak.

faq.question: Should I use a single document or multiple files?
faq.answer: Multiple files or modular pages are better. A single massive document is hard to navigate and slow to load on older Macs.

costs.title: Time loss
costs.text: Searching for the latest version of a document steals time from actual design work.

costs.title: Communication friction
costs.text: Misaligned team members lead to wasted effort and redundant meetings.

costs.title: Knowledge decay
costs.text: When a designer leaves, undocumented decisions are lost forever.

causes.title: The GDD trap
causes.text: Trying to document the entire game before production starts.

causes.title: Tool fragmentation
causes.text: Using too many different apps that do not talk to each other.

causes.title: Iterative reality
causes.text: Game design changes constantly, but static documents do not.

fixes.title: Modular structure
fixes.text: Break your document into smaller, linked pages based on specific mechanics.

fixes.title: Decision logs
fixes.text: Keep a simple list of why you made a design choice to avoid re-litigating it later.

fixes.title: Prototype as truth
fixes.text: If you are unsure about a mechanic, test it in the prototype rather than writing about it.
